heading: Choose what ty init creates
body:
`ty init` works like a project generator. In a terminal it asks five short questions, one at a time. Each question shows a numbered list. Type the numbers that you want, separated by commas, or press Enter to keep the answer in the question. The questions are: which parts the app has (a client with pages, a server, or both), which Tac languages the pages use, which Yon languages the server uses, where the app runs (the web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android), and which examples you want (storage, sockets, topics, streams, an HTTP client, error handlers). A question that does not fit your answers is skipped. For example, a server-only app has no page languages.

Every question is also an option, so a script can create the same app: `--realm`, `--tac`, `--yon`, `--target` and `--features`. When no terminal is attached and you give no options, `ty init` uses the defaults: both parts, JavaScript, and the web. `ty init` creates only the folders and files for your answers. Each language gets one small example class, a test unit that calls each public method, and a test setup, so `ty test --coverage` (on Node.js or Bun) and `ty preview` pass on the new app without any change. In a JavaScript or TypeScript app, `tsc -p client/jsconfig.json` and `tsc -p server/jsconfig.json` pass too, after `ty types` writes the composed types. The examples are written in JavaScript, or in TypeScript when TypeScript is the only JavaScript-family language that you chose. A Swift or Kotlin page service also gets a JavaScript copy, because Swift runs only in the Apple apps and Kotlin only in the Android app.

Then `ty init` checks the tools that your answers need, with the same checks as `ty doctor`. For each missing tool it shows the exact commands and asks before it runs them. It installs with each vendor's official installer into your home folder, for example rustup, the Go and Dart archives, the Bun archive, the .NET install script, SDKMAN for Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Gradle, emsdk for Emscripten, and the TinyGo and Binaryen archives, which make release WebAssembly smaller (see WebAssembly compilers per language). It uses versions that Tachyon is tested with, and it checks each download against the SHA-256 that the vendor publishes (Tachyon pins the emsdk and TinyGo hashes itself). It never runs a command with administrator rights: it prints such a command, for example `sudo apt-get install -y php-cgi`, and you run it yourself. Xcode and the Android SDK cannot be installed by a command, so `ty init` shows a link and the steps. `--yes` answers yes for every tool, and `--skip-tools` skips the check.

Later, `ty add` grows the app with the same examples, tests and tool check: `ty add language server py`, `ty add target ios` and `ty add feature sockets`. It never overwrites a file; it stops with TY1402 when a file that it would write already exists.
